summary:
Field Shift is a web-based decision-support tool that turns NASA Earth observations into crop-rotation guidance farmers can understand in seconds.

A farmer marks their field on an interactive satellite map and sets their priorities: water availability, machinery and preferred crops. Field Shift combines long-term climate from NASA POWER, vegetation and heat stress from ECOSTRESS, and elevation-based erosion risk with local soil information. It then compares three rotation strategies, including the current one. Each strategy shows traffic-light indicators for water, soil and risk, plus a plain-language explanation of why it was suggested, what evidence supports it, and where information is missing. Scenario sliders for rainfall and temperature let farmers explore “what if next year is drier?” and see the answer live.

This addresses the challenge directly: it makes climate adaptation tangible, explainable and accessible to people without technical or geospatial training. Machine-learning models were benchmarked across 11 agricultural concepts, but recommendations stay rule-based and transparent. The tool supports, and never replaces, farmer judgment and local expertise.

It matters because farmers now face decisions faster than experience can guide them. Field Shift brings the satellite’s view into the field, at no cost to the farmer.
details:
Field Shift: From Satellite Data to the Farmer’s Next Decision

Every season, a farmer makes a bet with the whole harvest: what to plant next? The wrong rotation drains water, depletes soil and exposes the field to heat, drought and erosion. The data to make a better choice exists, but it sits in scientific archives that no farmer will ever open.

Field Shift turns NASA Earth observations into a rotation decision a farmer can understand in seconds.

Mark your field on the map. The farmer draws or selects a parcel on an interactive satellite map.

We fuse the evidence. The system pulls long-term climate from NASA POWER, vegetation and water stress from ECOSTRESS, and elevation, slope and erosion potential from NASA elevation data. It combines these with local soil information.

The farmer sets their priorities: irrigated or rain-fed, available water, machinery, and which crops they prefer to sell.

Three rotation strategies are compared, including the current one. Each has traffic-light indicators for water, soil and risk, and a plain-language explanation of why it was suggested, what evidence supports it, where information is missing, and what must be reviewed locally.

Scenario sliders change the future. Move rainfall (e.g., −20%) or temperature (e.g., +2 °C) and the recommendations recalculate live. A farmer can ask “what if next year is drier?” and see the answer.

The platform also offers a global mode that shows observed climate for the visible map cells (NASA POWER), and live predictions from our ML service. If that service fails, the app does not break. It falls back to the latest data batch and clearly labels it as outdated.

Benefits

Soil health: favors rotations that cut bare-field periods, reduce erosion and add organic matter.

Water conservation: flags water-hungry choices before planting, not after the season is lost.

Resilience: stress-tests every strategy against hotter and drier futures.

Accessibility: no GIS or data-science skills needed. Maps, colors and short explanations replace tables and jargon.

Zero cost to use: built on open NASA data and deployable on free-tier infrastructure.

Trust: every recommendation is explainable and shows its uncertainty.

Intended impact

We want every farmer, from a family plot to a cooperative, to have the foresight that once took generations of experience, now that conditions are changing faster than experience can follow.

Near term: pilot in Durango, Mexico, with agricultural technicians and cooperatives, validating recommendations in the field.

Long term: since all parameters are configurable, expanding to a new region means changing coordinates and local crop data, not rewriting the system.

Field Shift supports and never replaces farmer judgment and local expertise. It highlights where human knowledge matters most and recommends consulting local technicians.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

Data: NASA POWER, ECOSTRESS, NASA elevation products. We also used USDA data (CDL, SSURGO, QuickStats), PRISM and ERA5 for soil, crop and climate context.

Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre GL (interactive maps), Recharts.

Backend: NestJS (TypeScript), GraphQL (Apollo), Prisma, PostgreSQL 16 + PostGIS for geospatial data.

Machine learning: Python, scikit-learn, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, PyTorch (LSTM/GRU/N-BEATS/PatchTST), Prophet, Optuna and MLflow for tuning and tracking.

Infrastructure: Docker, Render, Neon and Cloudflare, all on free tiers. Quality: automated unit, end-to-end and integration tests against real PostGIS; rate limiting and query depth/complexity limits for API security.

What makes it creative

Satellites in the farmer’s language. Our innovation is the translation layer: traffic lights, sliders and plain-language reasons built on real NASA science.

“What if” as a first-class feature. Climate sliders make adaptation tangible instead of abstract.

Rigorous AI, honestly used. We benchmarked more than 15 algorithms across 11 agricultural concepts (yield, drought, heat waves, soil moisture, rainfall, vulnerability and more), each against a simple baseline. The recommendation engine stays rule-based and explainable, with AI supplying inputs. A farmer deserves to know why, not to trust a black box.

Honesty built into the interface. Outdated data is labeled, information gaps are listed, and risks are flagged for local review.

Factors our team considered

Explainability over accuracy theater: farmers adopt what they can question.

Uncertainty: we show it, instead of hiding behind a single number.

Data availability: we trained on Weld County, Colorado, the zone with full coverage of the challenge’s resources, and designed the architecture to move to Durango and beyond. Validation with local field data is our next step.

Reliability: graceful degradation when services fail.

Cost and access: open data and free infrastructure so cost is never a barrier.

Security and privacy: validated configuration, no secrets in code, request limits, and protected service tokens that never reach the browser.

The human factor: the tool does not replace agronomists, cooperatives or a family’s decades of knowledge. It gives them better questions and better evidence.
